Evaluation of aeration pretreatment to prepare an inoculum for the
two-stage hydrogen and methane production process
Andrea Giordano a,b, Valentina Sarli b,c, Maria Cristina Lavagnolo c, Alessandro Spagni b,⇑
a Acqua & Sole s.r.l., Manzola Fornace, Corteolona, PV, Italy
b ENEA, Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and the Environment, Water Management Section, Bologna, Italy
c Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Padova, via Marzolo 9, 35131 Padova, Italy
h i g h l i g h t s
 Aerobic stress was assessed for selecting a H2-producing inoculum.
 The biochemical hydrogen potential was tested on waste of the food industry.
 The produced inoculum was effective in H2 and CH4 production in a two-stage process.
 A high energy recovery as H2 and CH4 from waste was achieved.

i n f o

a b s t r a c t
This study evaluates the effect of aeration pretreatment to prepare an inoculum for H2 and CH4 produc-
tion in a two-stage process. Moreover, the biochemical hydrogen potential and biochemical methane
potential of waste from the food industry in a two-stage process was assessed. The results conﬁrmed
the possibility of using an aerobic stress for selecting a hydrogen-producing inoculum. The inoculum
was fairly stable since no hydrogenotrophic–methanogenic activity was observed in 25 days. The yields
measured using glucose as substrate were of approximately 160 and 280NmLH2gCOD
1 of glucose for
hydrogen and methane, respectively, which are in agreement with other studies using heat-shock for
the pretreatment of the inoculum. When waste of the food industry (wheat milling) was used as sub-
strate, a lower H2 yield was achieved by the aerobically-pretreated inoculum if compared to heat-shock;
however, when combined with methane production in a two-stage process, much higher CH4 yield was
achieved.

1. Introduction
Over the last decade, considerable efforts have been spent to
develop environmentally sustainable technologies for hydrogen
production; in fact, whilst hydrogen is a clean energy carrier, now-
adays it is primarily produced using non-renewable fossil fuels
(Das and Veziroglu, 2001).
Biological hydrogen production can be performed through
photosynthetic
or
dark-fermentative
processes
(Das
and
Veziroglu, 2001). Several biotechnological processes which apply
different operating conditions (pure and mixed substrates, pure
and mixed cultures, batch and continuous reactors, etc.) have
recently been proposed for biological hydrogen production (Das
and Veziroglu, 2001). The use of mixed cultures seems to be more
promising as compared with pure cultures because they can be
easily adapted to different substrates belonging to renewable
resources or organic wastes. Moreover, well-developed and largely
applied technological systems for the anaerobic treatment of
wastewaters and organic solid wastes could be easily adapted for
hydrogen production (Li and Fang, 2007).
Although numerous bacteria are capable of producing hydro-
gen, during anaerobic processes hydrogen production is usually
not detected due to its rapid utilisation by other micro-organisms
(Das and Veziroglu, 2001). In performing biohydrogen production
tests, thus, the inoculum is usually thermally (mainly) or chemi-
cally pretreated in order to remove hydrogen-consumers whereas
hydrogen-producing bacteria are capable of surviving due to their
ability to produce spores (Li and Fang, 2007). However, these

pretreatments are very expensive hindering the application of the
process. Furthermore, the regrowth of hydrogenotrophic methano-
gens has sometimes been observed (Doungmanee et al., 2007;
Spagni et al., 2010), precluding or limiting the application of
continuous biohydrogen-producing systems. Spagni et al. (2010)
demonstrated the regrowth of methanogens can be hindered by
controlling the organic loading rate to the reactor. On the contrary,
Doungmanee et al. (2007) proposed to control the growth of meth-
anogens by repeated exposure of the sludge to high temperature
(90 C for 20 min).
Aeration has also been evaluated as pretreatment for harvesting
hydrogen producing biomass (Chang et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2008;
Wang and Wan, 2008; Zhu and Beland, 2006). Although aeration is
also an energy-demanding process it could easily be implemented
in many plants since blowers are already available in many sites
(e.g., in wastewater treatment plants). Moreover, the use of aera-
tion for controlling the process if the shift of H2-producing to
hydrogenotrophic–methanogenic conditions is observed seems to
be easier than the use of thermal pretreatment. In fact, aeration
requires blowers and diffusers that could be easily moved or are
even already available on-site, whilst thermal treatment also
requires equipment that must be resistant to heat-shock.
Since dark-fermentative processes produce volatile fatty acids
(VFAs) together with hydrogen, recently a two-step process has
been proposed where the produced VFAs are used as substrate
for biological methane production (Antonopoulou et al., 2008a,
2008b; Chu et al., 2012; Cooney et al., 2007; Hawkes et al., 2008;
Jung et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2009; Venkata Mohan et al., 2008; Xie
et al., 2008a, 2008b; Zhu et al., 2008). Some studies have also dem-
onstrated that the two-stage process for H2 and CH4 production
can increase the methane yield in the second stage likely due to
the improvement of hydrolysis in the ﬁrst stage (Liu et al., 2006;
Pakarinen et al., 2011).
Standardised methods for the determination of the biochemical
methane potential (BMP) of organic compounds have been applied
for a long time (Angelidaki et al., 2009) and similar batch tests have
also been proposed for evaluating the biochemical hydrogen
potential (BHP) of several substrates (e.g., Liu et al., 2013). More-
over, a batch test has recently been suggested for the determina-
tion of the hydrogen and methane potential for the two-stage
fermentative process (Giordano et al., 2011).
To the best knowledge of the authors, no studies have been per-
formed to assess aerobic pretreatment of inoculum for H2 and CH4
production in the two-stage process, and, in addition, to speciﬁ-
cally evaluate the ‘‘stability’’ of the hydrogen-producing biomass
(i.e., if hydrogen-consuming bacteria regrowth is observed). There-
fore, the aims of the present study are to: (i) evaluate the use of the
aerobic stress to develop a hydrogen-producing inoculum; (ii)
evaluate the ‘‘stability’’ of the hydrogen-producing inoculum (i.e.,
evaluate if hydrogenotrophic methanogens regrowth is observed);
and (iii) assess the BHP and BMP of organic wastes as a simulated
two-stage process (i.e., biohydrogen production followed by
biomethane production on the produced VFAs) by using the
prepared inoculum.
2. Methods
2.1. Substrates
Glucose (Carlo Erba reagents, Italy) was used as substrate for
both BHP and BMP tests. Moreover, two wastes from a typical Ital-
ian food industry (i.e., ﬂour mill processing) were used as feed-
stock: (i) wheat bran of Triticum durum for the production of the
durum wheat of the typical Italian pasta (produced in a ﬂour mill
in the province of Pavia, Northern Italy); (ii) wheat bran of Triticum
aestivum for the production of the common wheat bread (produced
in a ﬂour mill in the province of Alessandria, Northern Italy). Before
use, the wastes were stored at 20 C.
Total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) of the wheat bran (both
common and durum) were 88% and 84%, respectively.
2.2. Inoculum and aerobic pretreatment
Granular mesophilic sludge originating from a full-scale upﬂow
anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) treating waste of the food indus-
try (potato processing) was used as inoculum for the estimation of
the biochemical hydrogen and methane potential (Giordano et al.,
2011). The sludge had a TS and VS content of 124 ± 20 and
83 ± 8 g L1, respectively, whilst the pH was 7.3 ± 0.5.
Aerobic pretreatment was carried out maintaining approxi-
mately 2 L of the granular sludge continuously aerated in a
Plexiglas vessel using an aquarium blower and a porous stone.
Aeration was maintained at approximately 100 Lair Lsludge
1
h1. After
2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 days of aeration, the granular sludge
was used for the determination of the BHP.
The same granular sludge without pretreatment was used for
the determination of the BMP.
2.3. Hydrogen production using aerobic pretreated sludge
The experiments were conducted in batch mode, in 1 L Pyrex-
glass bottles maintained at constant temperature (35 ± 1 C) in a
thermostatic cabinet.
For every duration (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 days) of the aer-
obic pretreament, two bottles were prepared with 120 g (drip-wet
weight) of inoculum and 6.9 g of glucose. pH was corrected to
7.2 ± 0.1 by using sodium carbonate monohydrate (approximately
0.25–0.6 g). Tap water was added to reach the ﬁnal volume of
600 mL,
resulting
to
a
glucose
concentration
of
11.5 g L1
(12.305 g of COD (chemical oxygen demand) L1; 64 mmol L1).
The bottles were airtight sealed with screw caps (‘‘Omniﬁt C
series’’) which contained three valves for sampling. Anaerobic
conditions were achieved by ﬂushing the bottles with N2 for
approximately 5–10 min before the beginning of the experiments.
Two ‘‘blank’’ bottles were prepared as described above but
without the addition of glucose. All results have been expressed
as net values (subtracting the blank).
More details of the procedures, including the addition of macro-
and microelements, are reported elsewhere (Giordano et al., 2011).
2.4. Stability of the aerobic pretreated inoculum for biological
hydrogen production
For this experiment, three bottles (prepared as described in Sec-
tion 2.3) were ﬁlled with 120 g (drip-wet weight) of aerobically
(for 4 days) pretreated sludge, 6.9 g of glucose and tap water to a
ﬁnal volume of 600 mL. When glucose was depleted, also high-
lighted by the end of the biological hydrogen production, another
6.9 g of glucose was added twice consecutively (without any addi-
tional sludge).
The tests were performed at 35 ± 1 C.
Two
blank
bottles
were
also
arranged
as
described
in
Section 2.3.
2.5. Biochemical hydrogen potential (BHP) and subsequent
biochemical methane potential (BMP)
The experiments were conducted according to the method for
the estimation of BHP and BMP described in Giordano et al. (2011).
Three 1-L bottles were ﬁlled with 120 g of granular sludge aer-
obically pretreated (4 days of aeration), the substrates and tap

water to the ﬁnal volume of 600 mL. At the beginning of the test, if
necessary, pH was corrected to 7.2 ± 0.1 by adding Na2CO3H2O.
The substrates tested were two wastes of the food industry (see
Section 2.1) and glucose for comparison: the tests were performed
using approximately (the precise amounts were measured for each
bottle) 15–16 g of waste of the milling process.
The bottles were then airtight sealed using the same screw caps
(Omniﬁt C series) described above and incubated at 35 ± 1 C until
the end of the hydrogen production.
Then, for the evaluation of the BMP, 120 g of non-pretreated
granular sludge (therefore containing methanogenic bacteria)
were added to every bottle in order to assess the methane produc-
tion from the VFAs produced. Because of the pH decrease
measured during the hydrogen production processes, 1.6–2.5 g of
Na2CO3H2O were added to the bottles in order to increase the
pH to 7.2 ± 0.1 to optimise biomethane production.
Two blank bottles were arranged also in these experiments as
described in Section 2.3.
2.6. Analyses
Gas production was measured at room temperature using the
water displacement method in sodium hydroxide solution (1 M)
to allow carbon dioxide removal. The gas volumes were converted
to standard conditions (STP). The produced gas volume was
corrected by subtracting the production of the ‘‘blanks’’ bottles.
Liquid and gas samples were collected through the valves of the
screw caps. Gas was sampled from the headspace of the bottles
using an airtight 2-mL syringe. Liquid samples were centrifuged
for 15 min at 5000g and ﬁltered using nylon ﬁlters (Millipore) with
0.45 lm porosity. The mixed liquor samples were used for the
measurement of VFAs, glucose and pH.
Gas composition and VFAs (Acetic (HAc), propionic (HPr),
i- (HiBu) and n-butyric (HnBu), valeric (HVa), caproic (HCa) and
heptanoic (HHe) acids) were measured using gas-chromatographic
techniques as described in Spagni et al. (2010). VFAs were
expressed as COD for mass balance estimation, according to the
following equivalences (unit in g of COD/g of acid) reported by
Batstone et al. (2002): 1.07 for HAc, 1.51 for HPr, 1.82 for HnBu,
2.04 for HVa, 2.21 for HCa and 2.34 for HHe (note that HiBu was
never detected in this study).
pH was measured using Crison probes and pH-meter. TS and VS
were measured according to the Standard Methods (APHA et al.,
2005).
COD of the feedstock was estimated by the oxidation of approx-
imately 1 g of substrate with acidiﬁed dichromate according to the
open reﬂux method described in Standard Methods (APHA et al.,
2005).
Glucose was measured according to the phenol–sulphuric acid
method (Dubois et al., 1956). Glucose was also expressed in terms
of COD (gCODglu) using the equivalence of 1.07 g of COD/g of glucose.
2.7. Biogas yield estimation and mass balance
Several different units have been used to estimate the hydrogen
production yield, which makes comparison amongst substrates dif-
ﬁcult. In this study, the amount of electrons (as COD) were used for
mass balance and yield estimation as previously proposed in
Giordano et al. (2011); moreover, the estimations were carried
out on the basis of the substrates applied instead of the ones con-
verted because the amount of converted substrates cannot always
be determined for complex substrates (Kraemer and Bagley, 2005).
The equivalence of gCOD/g of VFAs, H2, CH4 and glucose was
assumed from Batstone et al. (2002).
The gas yields (as %) were also estimated, on COD basis, relative
to the initial amount of the substrates in order to evaluate the
fraction of the organic matter (as electron equivalence) that can
be converted to energetic gases, using the following equation:

Glucose and VFAs were also expressed in terms of COD (see

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect of the aerobic pretreatment on biohydrogen production
Continuous aeration for 2 days greatly altered the aspect of the
granules since their colour changed from dark-black (typical of the
anaerobic granular sludge) to bright brown–grey. Nevertheless, the
aerobic pretreatment lasting 2 days was not enough to completely
inhibit the hydrogenotrophic methanogens since the produced bio-
gas presented a signiﬁcant amount of methane (approximately
20%). As a result, the yield of hydrogen measured was of
67mLH2 g1
CODglu (Fig. 1).
The
hydrogen
yield
obtained
with
aeration
duration
of
3–12 days was higher than the previous one (aeration of 2 days),
showing values of 114—142mLH2 g1
CODglu. Biogas was mainly com-
posed of hydrogen with a concentration ranging from 60% to 70%
and the remaining part as CO2, whilst the methane concentration
was below the detection limit of the instrument (2%), conﬁrming
the effectiveness of the aerobic pretreatment in the selection of a
biomass capable to biologically produce hydrogen (Ren et al.,
2008).
The prolonged sludge aeration up to 14 days caused a decrease
of the measured H2 yield (76mLH2 g1
CODglu). However, contrary to the
aerobic pretreatment lasting 2 days, no methane was measured in
the biogas; moreover, no glucose was detected at the end of the
test conﬁrming that the substrate was completely depleted during
the fermentative metabolism. Therefore, a prolonged aerobic treat-
ment seemed to change the bacteria biochemical reactions to path-
ways not related to the biological hydrogen production. In fact it is
well-known that different fermentative pathways of monosaccha-
rides and acids can lead to different H2 yields (Li and Fang, 2007).
For example, 4 or 2 mol of H2 can be produced from the fermenta-
tion of glucose if the end products include acetic or butyric acid,
respectively; furthermore, some other fermentative end-products,

2010). However, since the VFAs were not monitored in this
experiment, the effect of duration of the aerobic pretreatment on

The obtained hydrogen yields of 114—142mLH2 g1
CODglu
are
equivalent to 1.0–1.2 mol of H2 per mol of glucose (molH2 mol1
glu),
which are included in the ranges obtained in previous studies
and applying similar operating conditions but using other pretreat-
ment (e.g., heat-shock) for the inoculum (Giordano et al., 2011; Li
and Fang, 2007). These results, on the contrary, are different to
those obtained by Chang et al. (2011) who achieved hydrogen pro-
duction by an aerobically-pretreated inoculum that were much
lower than those obtained by acid, base or heat-shock pretreat-
ment. Moreover, the same authors (Chang et al., 2011) applied an
aerobic pretreatment lasting 24 h which is 3 times lower than
was required in this study to completely inhibit methanogens.
However, they (Chang et al., 2011) used as inoculum the biomass
obtained by an activated sludge process (collected from an aerobic
wastewater treatment process) which was already acclimated to
aerobic conditions and supposedly lacking methanogenic activity.
Wang and Wan (2008) also found that 24 h of aeration of sludge
collected from a primary anaerobic digester were enough to select
for a hydrogen-producing inoculum: however, again, the hydrogen
yields obtained by aerobic pretreatment were much lower than
those obtained by heat-shock. Moreover, Zhu and Beland (2006)
showed that the aeration pretreatment of 30 min of sludge col-
lected from a primary anaerobic digester did not completely inhi-
bit methanogenic activity, conﬁrming that longer aeration should
be required to select for a hydrogen-producing inoculum. On the
contrary, Ren et al. (2008) reported the repeated-aeration (i.e., by
controlling dissolved oxygen concentration and the glucose feed)
as the most effective pretreatment method for selecting hydro-
gen-producing microbial community. This study, therefore, con-
ﬁrming the yields obtained in previous studies using as inoculum
the same anaerobic sludge but after thermal treatment (Giordano
et al., 2011), supports the ﬁnding that the inoculum source and
other factors, such as the duration or the intensity of the treatment,
greatly affected the efﬁcacy of the pretreatment (Ren et al., 2008; Li
et al., 2010).
The results show that 3–4 days were required to obtain hydro-
gen-producing biomass from anaerobic granular sludge. The long
time
needed
to
inhibit
the
hydrogenotrophic
methanogens
observed in this study can be explained by the strong physical rela-
tionship amongst micro-organisms in granular sludge. In fact, ther-
mal pretreatment has been also observed to be longer for
anaerobic granules than for anaerobic suspended sludge (Alibardi
et al., 2012). Furthermore, high tolerance of anaerobic granules
has also been previously described for acid conditions since meth-
anogens were found to be very active in hydrogen-producing sys-
tems operated at pH 4.5–5.5 (Spagni et al., 2010; Zhou and Ren,
2007).
3.2. Stability of the aerobic pretreated inoculum for biological
hydrogen production
The experiment was carried out using the granular sludge aer-
obically pretreated for 4 days.
Anaerobic glucose degradation showed a total hydrogen pro-

1122 ± 44 mL,

for the same pretreatment duration (4 days) suggesting a slight

With the second glucose load, a much lower yield than the ﬁrst
one was achieved, which reached the value of 46mLH2 g1
CODglu. The
third addition showed a H2 yield of 23mLH2 g1
CODglu, which was even
lower than the ﬁrst two (Fig. 2a). Biogas composition consisted of
hydrogen with a concentration of 60–70% with the remaining per-

Methane
concentrations were always below the detection limit of the
instrument for the entire duration of the experiment of 25 days.
Therefore, the aerobic pretreatment stably inhibited hydrogeno-
trophic methanogens at least for the duration of the experiment.
The results show that although methanogenic activity was not
observed, the second and the third glucose addition yielded a much
lower amount of hydrogen. Chemical analysis (data not shown)
revealed glucose consumption always above 94% at the end of each
load (i.e., just before the second and third load) suggesting that the
lower H2 production was not caused by a limited substrate utilisa-
tion. The VFAs trends demonstrated that different metabolic path-
ways were involved during the subsequent additions of substrates.
HnBu was the main acid produced during the fermentation of the
ﬁrst load of glucose, reaching the concentration of 33 mmol L1
(Fig. 2b). HAc showed a slightly lower concentration (30 mmol L1)
than HnBu. The other monitored acids, on the contrary, showed
very low concentrations with values usually lower than the detec-
tion limit of the instrument (0.05–0.1 mmol L1 depending on the
acid), with the exception of HCa which showed valued up to
4.0 mmol L1 just before the second glucose addition.
Acetic acid is the preferable end-product of the dark fermenta-
tive process since 4 mol of H2 can be theoretically obtained from
1 mol of glucose (Guo et al., 2010); microbial metabolism via the
butyrate pathway, instead, leads to a yield of 2molH2 mol1

The second glucose addition was characterised by a very high
build-up of propionic acid (Fig. 2b). Moreover, HAc concentration
increased further up to 50 molHAc L1, which exceeded the HnBu
values. Caproic acid, which was also detected during the ﬁrst load,
slightly accumulated after the second glucose load up to the con-
centration of 7.6 mmol L1.
Propionic acid is the product of a H2-consuming reaction (Guo
et al., 2010). The production of 28 mmol L1 of HPr could be related
to a consumption of an equivalent amount of H2 (Guo et al., 2010),
which resulted to a cumulative H2 consumption of 277 mL
(28 mmol L1  22.414 mL mmol1  0.6 L). Although HAc is usu-
ally considered as the preferable end-product of the biohydrogen
producing metabolism, several microbial species can also use that
acid

a
H2-consuming
process

a

addition, the concomitant increase of HAc and HPr observed for
the second glucose load, which resulted in a low H2 yield, could
also be justiﬁed by biochemical reactions which are neutral to
the
hydrogen
yield
such
as
the
lactic
acid
fermentation
(Antonopoulou et al., 2008a). However, since lactic acid was not
monitored in this study, this pathway cannot be conﬁrmed.
The third load was characterised by the formation of high-
weight VFAs such as HVa (up to 7.0 mmol L1) and HCa (up to
16.0 mmol L1), although a slight further increase of HAc and HnBu
was still observed. Propionic acid, on the contrary, remained
almost
stable
suggesting
that
the
HPr-producing
(i.e.,
an
H2-consuming process) metabolic pathways was not involved
during the third load.
It is of note that two peaks of HHe were observed just after the
second and third glucose addition (Fig. 2b). However, this long-
chain fatty acid was consumed during the fermentative metabo-
lism, likely with the production of shorter chain VFAs.
The formation of long-chain fatty acids can justify (at least to
some extent) the lower H2 yields of the second and third load than
the ﬁrst one. In fact, having a higher molecular weight and, thus, a
higher COD content, most of the electrons remained within the
organic matter instead of being directed to the H2 molecule.
Using the COD equivalences reported in Section 2.7, a COD mass
balance was carried out on the glucose fed to the system and the
products (H2 and VFAs) measured at the end of each load. This
mass balance revealed a limited COD closure (Fig. 2c). The COD
recovery as H2 was rather limited although in agreement with a
previous study (Giordano et al., 2011), showing recoveries from
10.1% of the ﬁrst load to 6.6% and 4.6% for the second and third
load, respectively. The COD recovery as VFAs also decreased from
66% to 59% and 49% measured for the ﬁrst, second and third glu-
cose load, respectively. It should be pointed out that the decreasing
total COD recovery (i.e., H2 and VFAs) passing from the ﬁrst (77%)
to the second (66%) and the third (54%) load supports the hypoth-
esis that other metabolic pathways could have been involved dur-
ing the subsequent glucose addition. In fact, other end-products of
the dark-fermentative processes (such as ethanol and lactic acid)
which are not involved in H2 producing process (and were not
monitored in this study) have also been described (Guo et al.,
2010).
Furthermore, several studies (e.g., Wang et al., 2008) have dem-
onstrated that the accumulation of end-products (e.g., ethanol,
acetic acid, lactic acid) of the fermentative metabolism can also
signiﬁcantly inhibit the biohydrogen production.
Hydrogen production caused a pH decrease from 7.7 to 4.7 after
the degradation of the ﬁrst amount of glucose. Because pH was not
corrected, since acidic conditions should improve biological H2
production (Li and Fang, 2007), it decreased to 4.2 with the second
glucose addition and remained stable with the third one. For bio-
logical hydrogen production by dark-fermentation, the optimal
pH value seems to be close to 5.5 (Li and Fang, 2007). Therefore,
the reduced hydrogen yields might also be caused by a partial inhi-
bition due to the very low pH values measured in the bottles.

conﬁrming the appropriateness of the used inoculum and the
applied pretreatment for hydrogen and methane production
(Fig. 3).

completely in agreement with the tests described in the previous

The hydrogen yields obtained from wastes of the food industry
by the fermentative process were, however, much lower than that
obtained from glucose, showing the values of 45.8 ± 0.4 and
29  3mLH2 g1
COD for durum and common wheat, respectively.
These values are lower than those obtained by Hawkes et al.
(2008) who reported yields of 54—91LH2 kg1
vs (55 and 33LH2 kg1
vs
in this study, using the same unit). These values are also lower than
the yields obtained by the same substrates in a previous study
using the same inoculum that was, however, treated by heat-shock
(Giordano et al., 2011). Therefore, the results of this study suggest
that a lower H2 yield is obtained when using an inoculum aerobi-
cally pretreated than when using thermal treatment. However,
with respect to the previous study (Giordano et al., 2011), the
industrial food waste was stored for approximately one year in
the laboratory before use and, thus, although the substrates were
relatively dry and stored at 20 C, a partial degradation could
have occurred. In addition, these differences could also be due to
waste heterogeneity.
It is noteworthy that, although the BHP tests lasted for almost
one week, more than 60% of hydrogen was produced in the ﬁrst
two days for all substrates, conﬁrming the high activity of the
H2-producing microorganisms (Giordano et al., 2011).
As expected, VFAs were produced during the biological hydro-
gen production process, and promptly degraded by methanogenic
bacteria (Fig. 4). HnBu and HAc were the two main VFAs produced
for all substrates. However, whilst HnBu was the main fatty acid
produced during the fermentation of glucose, HAc predominated
when the two wastes were used as feed. In spite of this, the
fermentation of the two wastes resulted in much lower H2 yields.
Furthermore, the highest HAc concentration was observed during
the fermentation of the common wheat (Fig. 4c), which, however,
showed the lowest H2 yield amongst the three tested substrates.
This result suggests that fermentative pathways that produce ace-
tic acids but do not yield H2 or even consume H2 (Antonopoulou
et al., 2008a; Guo et al., 2010) could be involved during the fermen-
tation of the investigated waste by aerobically-treated anaerobic
granules.
The other monitored VFAs always showed very low concentra-
tions, conﬁrming that their production occurred with extremely
high load and at acidic conditions as measured during the previous
experiment (see Section 3.2).
The results conﬁrm the effectiveness of using the VFAs pro-
duced by the biological hydrogen production process as substrate
for methane production via anaerobic processes (Giordano et al.,
2011; Antonopoulou et al., 2008a,b).
The VFAs were completely consumed in 4–7 days under meth-
anogenic conditions (i.e., after 11–14 days of the experiment in
Fig. 4), conﬁrming the high activity of methanogens contained in
the (non-pretreated) inoculum. However, the methane production
rates were very different amongst the three substrates (Fig. 3). In
fact, whilst in the same period (4–7 days) more than 95% of the
methane yield was obtained when glucose was used as substrate
(Fig. 3a), approximately 72% and 65% of the total CH4 yields were
obtained for durum and common wheat, respectively (Fig. 3b and
c). This result demonstrates that, when glucose was used as sub-
strate, methane production was completely performed on the VFAs
produced during the ﬁrst H2-producing step, whilst, during the fer-
mentation of the two wastes, a signiﬁcant amount of methane was
produced from the organic matter that seemed to be still contained

Table 1 reports the gas recovery (as deﬁned in Eq. (1)) obtained
in this study and some data from the literature for comparison. As
already stated (Giordano et al., 2011; Kraemer and Bagley, 2005),
the commonly used units for determination of the hydrogen yield
(e.g., mol gas on mol of glucose or hexose) make difﬁcult the com-
parison amongst different materials (such as wastes). Therefore,
the recovery concept proposed by Kraemer and Bagley (2005) as
adopted by Giordano et al. (2011) was also used in this study. A
similar approach, by using electron-equivalent balance, was also
adopted by Cota-Navarro et al. (2011) in evaluation the H2 and
CH4 yields treating cheese whey powder.
The total gas (H2 and CH4) recovery from glucose (92.0%)
approximates the mass balance closure if a biomass growth yield
of 0.1 gCOD of biomass per gCOD of substrate (Batstone et al.,
2002) is assumed. The check of the mass balance conﬁrms that
an increase of the biohydrogen production to the maximum exper-
imental yield of 2:5molH2 mol1
glu (Li and Fang, 2007; Guo et al.,
2010) has to result in a decrease of the methane recovery
(Giordano et al., 2011).
The gas recovery also conﬁrms that much more energy could be
gained from the wastes. In fact, gas recovery comprised from 22%
and 91% has been observed (Table 1) depending on the nature of
the used waste, inoculum, technology and operating conditions.
It has to be highlighted, that the aerobic pretreatment of the
inoculum seems to signiﬁcantly improve the total gas recovery
(10–18%) if compared to the same waste when the inoculum was
thermally pretreated (Table 1). This improvement could be
explained by substrate heterogeneity or by a partial hydrolysis of
the wastes during storage. However, the improvement might also
be due to better hydrolysis activity of the used inoculum. In fact,
although the aim of the pretreatments of the inoculum is the inhi-
bition of methanogens, the pretreatments can also inhibit most of
the populations forming the microbial community. For example,

thermal pretreatment (as other strong treatments) select for
microorganisms that are able to produce spores. Since many
hydrogen-producing microorganisms are able to form spores
whilst methanogens are not (Li and Fang, 2007), pretreatment such
as heat-shock is often selective for a H2-producing inoculum (Li
and Fang, 2007). However, the same pretreatments could also
severely affect other bacteria which could have high hydrolytic
activity, reducing, therefore, the capacity to degrade complex sub-
strates such as waste or energy crops. The results of this study
which show low H2 and high gas (as the sum of H2 and CH4) yields
(Table 1), thus, suggest that the aeration pretreatment may be less
effective than other methods in selecting for a H2-producing inoc-
ulum whilst, on the contrary, could be more suitable in preserving
the hydrolytic activity which could results from a more structured
microbial community. Although a speciﬁc investigation on the
microbial community was not conducted in this study, Ren et al.
(2008) demonstrated that different pretreatments (thermal, chem-
ical, aeration) led to signiﬁcant and diverse microbial population
shift in the inoculum. Moreover, the same authors (Ren et al.,
2008) also found that, amongst the pretreatments they tested,
the aerobic pretreatment ensured the highest microbial diversity,
supporting, therefore, the hypothesis proposed in this study.
Pakarinen et al. (2011) achieved an increase up to 64% in CH4
yield by the addition of a thermophilic H2-producing step before
a mesophilic methanogenic stage in a two-stage process treating
grass silage or maize. However, the H2 production was always
much lower than that of CH4 (from 0.7% to 6.0% in volume) con-
ﬁrming the results of this study that a high CH4 yield is obtained
when H2 production is relatively low.
4. Conclusions
The results of this study conﬁrm the possibility of using an
aerobic stress for selecting a H2-producing inoculum. The yields
measured using glucose as substrate were of approximately
160 and 280mLH2 g1
CODglu for H2 and CH4, respectively, which are
in agreement with other studies using heat-shock for harvesting
an H2-producing inoculum.
When waste of the food industry was used as feed, the aerated
inoculum achieved a slightly lower H2 yield if compared to heat-
shock; however, when combined with methane production in a
two-stage process, much higher CH4 yield was achieved suggesting
a higher hydrolytic activity of the selected inoculum.
